plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a single upward-opening parabola on a coordinate plane and annotates its main features with labeled arrows. Both axes are numbered from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid, with x labeled at the right end of the horizontal axis and y at the top of the vertical one. The curve is a heavy teal U with arrowheads on both rising branches; its lowest point sits at x equal to 1, y equal to -4, and the branches climb to about y equal to 5 near x equal to -2 on the left and x equal to 4 on the right. Small filled dots mark the two crossings of the x-axis at x equal to -1 and x equal to 3, the crossing of the y-axis at y equal to -3, the turning point, and the mirror partner of the y-intercept at x equal to 2. A red dashed vertical line runs through x equal to 1, reached by an arrow from the label Axis of symmetry above. Three further labels point to the graph and read x-intercepts, y-intercept, and Vertex. Drawing the dashed line through the turning point lets the reader check that the marked dots sit at equal heights on either side. The graph fixes the vocabulary for reading a quadratic.

demo_steps.title: Read the intercepts
demo_steps.narration: The highlighted intercepts show where the parabola crosses the axes: the x-intercepts are the zeros of the quadratic, and the y-intercept is the value when x = 0.

demo_steps.title: Find the symmetry
demo_steps.narration: The dashed red line passes through the vertex and splits the parabola into two matching sides. Points at the same height, such as the y-intercept and its partner, sit the same horizontal distance from this line.

demo_steps.title: Move the vertex
demo_steps.narration: Drag the vertex to a new position. The dashed axis of symmetry moves with it, showing that the vertex fixes the turning point and the line of symmetry.

demo_steps.title: Change the opening width
demo_steps.narration: Use the vertical stretch slider to make the parabola narrower or wider. The axis remains fixed through the vertex, but the x-intercepts shift inward or outward depending on the stretch.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The vertex is the anchor of a parabola: it sets the turning point and axis of symmetry, while the vertical stretch changes how quickly the branches rise and therefore where the intercepts occur.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original graph as y = (x - 1)^2 - 4 on a square coordinate grid, with a teal curve, black feature dots, and a red dashed axis of symmetry at x = 1. Use the drag interaction to update the vertex form y = a(x - h)^2 + k, keeping the dashed line at x = h and recomputing the intercepts and mirror point dynamically. Use the slider as the coefficient a, with default a = 1. In intercept focus, visually emphasize the x-intercepts and y-intercept with brighter halos and stronger arrows; in symmetry focus, emphasize the vertex, dashed symmetry line, and paired equal-height points on opposite sides of the axis.

authoredContext:
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. One important feature of the graph is that it has an extreme point, called the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex represents the lowest point on the graph, or the minimum value of the quadratic function. If the parabola opens down, the vertex represents the highest point on the graph, or the maximum value. In either case, the vertex is a turning point on the graph. The graph is also symmetric with a vertical line drawn through the vertex, called the axis of symmetry. These features are illustrated in the figure.

Graph of a parabola showing where the x and y intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry are.

The y-intercept is the point at which the parabola crosses the y-axis. The x-intercepts are the points at which the parabola crosses the x-axis. If they exist, the x-intercepts represent the zeros, or roots, of the quadratic function, the values of x at which y=0.

discrepancies: The two black reference points on the upper arms of the parabola, near (−2, 5) and (4, 5), are missing; the generated curve has arrowheads but not those marked points.
The default view adds yellow highlight halos around the intercepts and uses brown/gold leader arrows, while the source uses plain black dots and black annotation arrows with no highlighting.
The red dashed axis of symmetry continues down to the bottom of the grid, whereas in the source it stops shortly below the vertex.
The generated y-intercept and x-intercepts callout arrows are repositioned and more visually dominant than in the source, changing the balance of the annotation layout.
The source’s static textbook look is partly replaced by interactive emphasis styling, so the default state is not a clean drop-in replacement for the original figure.
evaluation.notes: The parabola, intercepts, vertex, axis of symmetry, grid, and main labels are mostly accurate, but the default interactive highlighting and missing upper branch points reduce fidelity to the source.
action_items: Add the two black marked points on the upper branches at approximately (−2, 5) and (4, 5), matching the source.
Remove or disable the yellow intercept halos in the default state so the initial view matches the static textbook figure.
Use black leader arrows for the labels by default instead of brown/gold emphasis arrows.
Shorten the red dashed axis of symmetry so it ends just below the vertex rather than continuing to the bottom of the grid.
